title: He will come again
hookLine: the creeds say Christ will return; churches differ on how and when

lines: THIS SAME JESUS SHALL SO COME.
cards: A group of friends stands on a hill, staring at the sky. Jesus has just been taken up out of their sight, and they're still looking.

Then two men in white are beside them: "Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven? this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven."
The creeds keep that promise. Churches have read it in different ways: some with urgency, some with quiet patience, some with careful timelines.

teach.b: The creeds say it in a line. The Apostles' Creed: "From thence he shall come to judge the quick and the dead." The quick means the living.
One New Testament Greek word for his coming is parousia: an arrival, a presence. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches that say the creeds share that hope. Where they differ is how, and when.

teach.h: A THOUSAND YEARS, READ TWO WAYS.
teach.b: Revelation speaks of a thousand years in which Christ reigns.

teach.h: OF THAT DAY KNOWETH NO MAN.
teach.b: Some read that as a future age that begins when he returns. Others read it as now: the time of the church, between his first coming and his second.

Some evangelical churches teach that believers will first be caught up to meet him, often called the rapture, drawing on Paul's words about meeting the Lord in the air. Other churches read those same words differently.
And the date? Jesus is plain: "But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only." So the stance the Gospels ask for is not calculation but readiness.
Jesus tells of servants who keep their lights burning, waiting up for their master.
And near the Bible's very end comes a short prayer: "Even so, come, Lord Jesus." Paul, closing his first letter to Corinth, leaves an Aramaic word untranslated: maranatha.
Readers take it two ways: our Lord, come, or our Lord has come. Some readers hear both in it: he came, and he will come.

how: Christians who say the Apostles' or Nicene Creed confess that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead, and the season of Advent looks toward his coming; churches differ on how they read the details in Revelation and Paul.

games.q: what does “he will come again” mean?
o: a hope that the dead come back to visit us
the creeds' promise that Christ will return
a promise that Jesus will be born a second time

games.q: the words of the waiting — tap the pairs.
p: why stand ye gazing up into heaven?
Greek for his coming, an arrival
an Aramaic word Paul leaves as it is

s: Jesus gave his followers the date of his return
"of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only."
churches that say the creeds share the hope of his return
"from thence he shall come to judge the quick and the dead."
churches all read Revelation's thousand years the same way
some read it as a future age after he returns; others as the time of the church, now.

games.q: you're one of the friends on the hill. Jesus has been taken up, and you're staring at the sky. two men in white appear. what do they say?
o: "why stand ye gazing up into heaven?"
games.why: they turn the friends' eyes from the sky: "this same Jesus... shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven."

practice: Jesus tells of servants with their lights burning, awake when their master knocks: not frightened, ready.
So ask quietly, if today were the day, what would I want to have done, who would I call, what would I put down, and let one answer come clearly.
If you pray, use the prayer near the Bible's end, even so, come, Lord Jesus; if you don't, just hold the question.
